Strict Hausdorff-dimension drop for
Quartic Salem Bernoulli convolutions

Guozheng Cheng Address: School of Mathematical Sciences, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian, 116024, P. R. China Email address: gzhcheng@dlut.edu.cn , Xiang Fang Address: Department of Applied Mathematics, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Hsinchu, 300093, Taiwan Email address: xfang@nycu.edu.tw , Xueqing Ma Address: School of Mathematical Sciences, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian, 116024, P. R. China Email address: maxueqing4680@mail.dlut.edu.cn and Hongli Zhang Address: School of Mathematical Sciences, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian, 116024, P. R. China Email address: zhanghongli1@mail.dlut.edu.cn
Abstract.

For every quartic Salem number β\beta, we prove that the equal-weight Bernoulli convolution νβ−1\nu_{\beta^{-1}} has Hausdorff dimension strictly less than one. The main step converts large Fourier coefficients at geometrically separated frequencies into a deficit in the Shannon entropy of a finite convolution. A positive trigonometric product gives the entropy estimate, while the algebraic norm controls the number of distinct atoms in each spatial cell. For the two quartic Salem numbers in (1,2)(1,2), reciprocal differences at suitable return times produce the required Fourier coefficients. A finite block cover then gives the dimension bound. This proof is independent of numerical computation. Separate exact calculations give dimHνβ1−1<1−1.4⋅10−23\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\nu_{\beta_{1}^{-1}}<1-1.4\cdot 10^{-23} and dimHνβ2−1<1−7.8⋅10−22\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\nu_{\beta_{2}^{-1}}<1-7.8\cdot 10^{-22}, where β1<β2\beta_{1}<\beta_{2} are the two parameters in (1,2)(1,2). The accompanying verification programs use rational interval arithmetic and the Python standard library.

Key words and phrases: 
Bernoulli convolution, Salem number, Hausdorff dimension, Shannon entropy, Fourier transform, rigorous computation

1. Introduction

This paper is a sequel to [3]. For β>1\beta>1, let

W=∑k=0∞εk​β−k,νβ−1=Law⁡(W),ℙ⁡(εk=1)=ℙ⁡(εk=−1)=12,W=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\varepsilon_{k}\beta^{-k},\qquad\nu_{\beta^{-1}}=\Law(W),\qquad\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon_{k}=1)=\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon_{k}=-1)=\frac{1}{2},

where the signs are independent. The subscript denotes the contraction ratio. Bernoulli convolutions form a basic family of self-similar measures whose regularity depends on the arithmetic of this ratio. For β>2\beta>2, the elementary dimension bound dimHνβ−1≤log⁡2/log⁡β\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\nu_{\beta^{-1}}\leq\log 2/\log\beta is already strictly below one. The question considered here lies in the overlapping range 1<β<21<\beta<2.

We study quartic Salem parameters. A Salem number is a real algebraic integer β>1\beta>1 whose other conjugates consist of β−1\beta^{-1} and one or more pairs on the unit circle. In degree four there is exactly one such pair, denoted by ζ,ζ¯\zeta,\bar{\zeta}. The contribution of this pair to an algebraic orbit is an oscillation that does not decay. Controlling this term while keeping the cost of the remaining orbit small is the main difficulty in the construction below.

There are two closely related regularity results to distinguish. In [3] we prove a strict drop in correlation dimension for the two quartic Salem parameters in (1,2)(1,2). The preprint [5, Theorem 5.1] establishes singularity for the same parameters by a Fourier-analytic argument. We emphasize that [5] is cited only for comparison: neither the proof of Theorem 1.1 nor the rigorous computations underlying Theorem 1.2 rely on any result from that preprint. Our localization argument starts from the reciprocal-orbit construction in [3]. Neither singularity nor a strict drop in correlation dimension alone implies a strict drop in Hausdorff dimension. Our aim is to prove this stronger dimension conclusion and to give explicit positive bounds for the two deficits.

The distinction leads us to Shannon entropy. Garsia [4] related the entropy of finite Bernoulli convolutions to singularity, and Akiyama, Feng, Kempton, and Persson [1] developed matrix methods for the entropy of algebraic Bernoulli convolutions. Here we obtain a finite entropy deficit directly from Fourier coefficients. The argument uses the exact distribution of the finite sum, with coincident atoms identified, and ends with an explicit Hausdorff cover.

For a Borel probability measure μ\mu on ℝ\mathbb{R}, we use the convention

dimHμ=inf{dimHA:A⊂ℝ​ is Borel and ​μ​(A)=1}.\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\mu=\inf\{\dim_{\mathrm{H}}A:A\subset\mathbb{R}\text{ is Borel and }\mu(A)=1\}.

Translating and rescaling to digits {0,1}\{0,1\}, or starting the series at k=1k=1, does not change this dimension. The two quartic Salem numbers in (1,2)(1,2) are the larger real roots β1<β2\beta_{1}<\beta_{2} of

P1​(X)=X4−X3−X2−X+1,P2​(X)=X4−2​X3+X2−2​X+1.\begin{split}P_{1}(X)&=X^{4}-X^{3}-X^{2}-X+1,\\ P_{2}(X)&=X^{4}-2X^{3}+X^{2}-2X+1.\end{split} (1.1)

Equivalently,

u1=1+132,u2=1+2,βi=ui+ui2−42.u_{1}=\frac{1+\sqrt{13}}{2},\qquad u_{2}=1+\sqrt{2},\qquad\beta_{i}=\frac{u_{i}+\sqrt{u_{i}^{2}-4}}{2}.

We include the elementary classification in Proposition 3.1.

Theorem 1.1.

For every quartic Salem number β\beta,

dimHνβ−1<1.\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\nu_{\beta^{-1}}<1.

In particular, each of the two measures corresponding to (1.1) gives full mass to a Borel set of dimension strictly below one and is therefore singular. The proof of Theorem 1.1 is independent of numerical computation. The following estimates come from separate finite calculations.

Theorem 1.2.

For the two parameters in (1.1),

dimHνβ1−1<1−1.4⋅10−23,dimHνβ2−1<1−7.8⋅10−22.\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\nu_{\beta_{1}^{-1}}<1-1.4\cdot 10^{-23},\qquad\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\nu_{\beta_{2}^{-1}}<1-7.8\cdot 10^{-22}.

The displayed numbers are lower bounds for the deficits 1−dimHνβi−11-\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\nu_{\beta_{i}^{-1}}. The finite inequalities underlying Theorem 1.2 are proved in the appendices and checked by the accompanying programs.

1.1. The entropy estimate and the proof

Write

XN=∑k=0N−1εk​β−k,R=ββ−1.X_{N}=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\varepsilon_{k}\beta^{-k},\qquad R=\frac{\beta}{\beta-1}.

Let ANA_{N} be the set of distinct values of XNX_{N}, and put px=ℙ⁡(XN=x)p_{x}=\mathbb{P}(X_{N}=x) for x∈ANx\in A_{N}. Its Shannon entropy is

HN=H(XN)=−∑x∈ANpxlogpx.H_{N}=H(X_{N})=-\sum_{x\in A_{N}}p_{x}\log p_{x}.

All logarithms are natural. We first prove that MM Fourier coefficients of modulus at least aa, at suitable geometrically separated frequencies below the scale βN\beta^{N}, imply

HN≤N​log⁡β−12​M​a2+2​log⁡N+Cβ.H_{N}\leq N\log\beta-\frac{1}{2}Ma^{2}+2\log N+C_{\beta}.

The gain comes from a positive trigonometric product. Its integral over a bounded interval stays bounded, whereas the expected value of its logarithm is large under the Bernoulli convolution. Relative entropy then gives an estimate on spatial cells. The algebraic norm bounds the number of distinct finite-convolution atoms in a cell by a constant multiple of N2N^{2}, accounting for the term 2​log⁡N2\log N.

We next construct the Fourier coefficients needed to make the gain larger than this logarithmic cost. The Fourier transform of νβ−1\nu_{\beta^{-1}} is a product of cosines. At the frequencies used below, the negative logarithm of its squared modulus is a sum of the potential V⁡(t)=−log⁡cos2⁡(π​t)V(t)=-\log\cos^{2}(\pi t) along a canonical algebraic orbit.

The unit-circle conjugates contribute a nondecaying oscillation to the right tail of such an orbit. Removing that term produces a localized sequence HH with two geometrically decaying real tails. We define its action by

E=∑j∈ℤV⁡(Hj).E=\sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}}V(H_{j}).

We start from fixed power seeds whose values at the unit-circle conjugates are small. Reciprocal differences at suitable return times then produce localized orbits with actions EkE_{k}, outgoing amplitudes Δk\Delta_{k}, and expanding coefficients ckc_{k} satisfying

Δk⟶0,Ek=o⁡(log⁡1Δk),0<c∗≤|ck|≤h<1100.\Delta_{k}\longrightarrow 0,\qquad E_{k}=o\!\left(\log\frac{1}{\Delta_{k}}\right),\qquad 0<c_{*}\leq|c_{k}|\leq h<\frac{1}{100}.

The constants c∗c_{*} and hh are independent of kk. The initial power seeds are specified in Lemma 3.4.

Restoring the outgoing oscillation gives large Fourier coefficients over a long interval of orbit indices. The preceding entropy estimate then yields HN<N​log⁡βH_{N}<N\log\beta at one fixed finite scale. Finally, an independent block cover gives

dimHνβ−1≤HNN​log⁡β<1.\dim_{\mathrm{H}}\nu_{\beta^{-1}}\leq\frac{H_{N}}{N\log\beta}<1.

Thus the strict dimension bound follows from a finite entropy deficit; the proof does not require an exact-dimensionality theorem or the calculation of an infinite entropy rate.

The explicit dimension bounds are obtained from finite configurations built from the same power seeds. Bounds on their action and outgoing amplitudes yield the required finite inequalities, which are checked using exact rational interval arithmetic. The large entropy block lengths are handled symbolically: the verification uses the proved estimates rather than enumerating the digit words.

Section 2 establishes the entropy and covering estimates. Sections 3–5 construct the localized orbits and control their action. Section 6 uses these orbits to prove Theorem 1.1. Appendices A and B prove the explicit bounds, and Appendix C describes their exact verification.

For the remainder of the proof, β\beta is one of β1,β2\beta_{1},\beta_{2} unless stated otherwise, ν=νβ−1\nu=\nu_{\beta^{-1}}, and ν^​(t)=𝔼​ei​t​W\widehat{\nu}(t)=\mathbb{E}e^{itW}.

2. Finite Fourier biases and Hausdorff covers

We first turn a finite family of Fourier lower bounds into an upper bound for HNH_{N}. We estimate entropy on a spatial grid, then use the algebraic norm to pass from cells to the distinct atoms of XNX_{N}.

Throughout this section, β>1\beta>1 is a quartic Salem number, with conjugates β,r=β−1,ζ,ζ¯\beta,r=\beta^{-1},\zeta,\bar{\zeta}. We write ν=νβ−1\nu=\nu_{\beta^{-1}} and R=β/(β−1)R=\beta/(\beta-1). The variables WW, XNX_{N} and the entropy HNH_{N} are as in the introduction; equal atoms are merged before entropy is computed.

Lemma 2.1.

Let Q>2Q>2, 0<a≤1/20<a\leq 1/2, and let M,NM,N be positive integers. Suppose that positive real frequencies satisfy

ξ1≥π,ξj+1≥Qξj,β−NξM≤1,|ν^(ξj)|≥a(1≤j≤M).\xi_{1}\geq\pi,\qquad\xi_{j+1}\geq Q\xi_{j},\qquad\beta^{-N}\xi_{M}\leq 1,\qquad|\widehat{\nu}(\xi_{j})|\geq a\quad(1\leq j\leq M).

Set

Ψ⁡(a)=(1+a)​log⁡(1+a)+(1−a)​log⁡(1−a)2,cQ=Q−2Q−1,\Psi(a)=\frac{(1+a)\log(1+a)+(1-a)\log(1-a)}{2},\qquad c_{Q}=\frac{Q-2}{Q-1},
DQ,a\displaystyle D_{Q,a} =2​aπ​cQ​(1−(1+a)/Q),\displaystyle=\frac{2a}{\pi c_{Q}(1-(1+a)/Q)},
BQ,a\displaystyle B_{Q,a} =a​Q(1−a)​(Q−1),\displaystyle=\frac{aQ}{(1-a)(Q-1)},
Csep\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{sep}} =1+1+2​R2​(β−1),\displaystyle=1+\frac{1+2R}{2(\beta-1)},

and

Cβ,Q​(a)=log⁡[(2​R+2+DQ,a)​Csep]+BQ,a.C_{\beta,Q}(a)=\log\!\bigl[(2R+2+D_{Q,a})C_{\mathrm{sep}}\bigr]+B_{Q,a}.

Then

HN\displaystyle H_{N} ≤N​log⁡β−M​Ψ​(a)+2​log⁡N+Cβ,Q​(a)\displaystyle\leq N\log\beta-M\Psi(a)+2\log N+C_{\beta,Q}(a)
≤N​log⁡β−12​M​a2+2​log⁡N+Cβ,Q​(a).\displaystyle\leq N\log\beta-\frac{1}{2}Ma^{2}+2\log N+C_{\beta,Q}(a). (2.1)

In particular, if β2>2\beta^{2}>2 and Q=β2Q=\beta^{2}, there is a finite constant Cβ>0C_{\beta}>0, independent of a,M,Na,M,N, such that

HN≤N​log⁡β−12​M​a2+2​log⁡N+Cβ.H_{N}\leq N\log\beta-\frac{1}{2}Ma^{2}+2\log N+C_{\beta}. (2.2)
Proof.

Since ν\nu is symmetric, its Fourier transform is real and ν^​(ξj)=𝔼​cos⁡(ξj​W)\widehat{\nu}(\xi_{j})=\mathbb{E}\cos(\xi_{j}W). We may therefore choose σj∈{−1,1}\sigma_{j}\in\{-1,1\} so that

𝔼⁡[σj​cos⁡(ξj​W)]≥a(1≤j≤M).\mathbb{E}[\sigma_{j}\cos(\xi_{j}W)]\geq a\qquad(1\leq j\leq M).

Consider the positive trigonometric product

𝒫⁡(x)=∏j=1M(1+a​σj​cos⁡(ξj​x)),F⁡(x)=log⁡𝒫⁡(x).\mathcal{P}(x)=\prod_{j=1}^{M}(1+a\sigma_{j}\cos(\xi_{j}x)),\qquad F(x)=\log\mathcal{P}(x).

Every factor lies between 1−a1-a and 1+a1+a, so FF is well defined. By concavity of the logarithm, for −1≤t≤1-1\leq t\leq 1,

log⁡(1+a​t)≥1+t2​log⁡(1+a)+1−t2​log⁡(1−a).\log(1+at)\geq\frac{1+t}{2}\log(1+a)+\frac{1-t}{2}\log(1-a).

The right-hand side is increasing in tt. Taking t=σj​cos⁡(ξj​W)t=\sigma_{j}\cos(\xi_{j}W) and using the choice of σj\sigma_{j}, we obtain

𝔼​log⁡(1+a​σj​cos⁡(ξj​W))≥1+a2​log⁡(1+a)+1−a2​log⁡(1−a)=Ψ⁡(a).\mathbb{E}\log(1+a\sigma_{j}\cos(\xi_{j}W))\geq\frac{1+a}{2}\log(1+a)+\frac{1-a}{2}\log(1-a)=\Psi(a).

Summing over jj gives 𝔼​F​(W)≥M​Ψ​(a)\mathbb{E}F(W)\geq M\Psi(a). Moreover, Ψ⁡(0)=Ψ′​(0)=0\Psi(0)=\Psi^{\prime}(0)=0 and Ψ′′​(a)=1/(1−a2)≥1\Psi^{\prime\prime}(a)=1/(1-a^{2})\geq 1. Consequently,

𝔼​F​(W)≥M​Ψ​(a)≥12​M​a2.\mathbb{E}F(W)\geq M\Psi(a)\geq\frac{1}{2}Ma^{2}.

We next estimate the integral of 𝒫\mathcal{P} over a bounded interval. Write each factor as

1+a​σj​cos⁡(ξj​x)=1+a​σj2​ei​ξj​x+a​σj2​e−i​ξj​x.1+a\sigma_{j}\cos(\xi_{j}x)=1+\frac{a\sigma_{j}}{2}e^{i\xi_{j}x}+\frac{a\sigma_{j}}{2}e^{-i\xi_{j}x}.

In the expansion of the product, consider a nonconstant term and let jj be the largest index at which a nonconstant summand was chosen. Its frequency ω\omega satisfies

|ω|≥ξj−∑i<jξi≥ξj−ξjQ−1=cQ​ξj>0,|\omega|\geq\xi_{j}-\sum_{i<j}\xi_{i}\geq\xi_{j}-\frac{\xi_{j}}{Q-1}=c_{Q}\xi_{j}>0,

where we used ξi+1≥Q​ξi\xi_{i+1}\geq Q\xi_{i}. Thus no nonconstant term in the expansion has zero frequency, and the constant term is one.

For a fixed largest index jj, the sum of the absolute values of the corresponding coefficients is a​(1+a)j−1a(1+a)^{j-1}. Indeed, the two nonconstant summands in the jj-th factor have total absolute coefficient aa, while each preceding factor contributes a total of 1+a1+a. For any bounded interval II and any ω≠0\omega\neq 0,

|∫Iei​ω​x​𝑑x|≤2|ω|.\left|\int_{I}e^{i\omega x}\,dx\right|\leq\frac{2}{|\omega|}.

Applying this estimate term by term, and using ξj≥Qj−1​ξ1\xi_{j}\geq Q^{j-1}\xi_{1} and ξ1≥π\xi_{1}\geq\pi, gives

|∫I𝒫⁡(x)​𝑑x−|I||\displaystyle\left|\int_{I}\mathcal{P}(x)\,dx-|I|\right| ≤∑j=1M2​a​(1+a)j−1cQ​ξj\displaystyle\leq\sum_{j=1}^{M}\frac{2a(1+a)^{j-1}}{c_{Q}\xi_{j}}
≤2​acQ​ξ1​∑j=1M(1+aQ)j−1≤DQ,a.\displaystyle\leq\frac{2a}{c_{Q}\xi_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\left(\frac{1+a}{Q}\right)^{j-1}\leq D_{Q,a}. (2.3)

Here the geometric series converges since (1+a)/Q<1(1+a)/Q<1.

We also need to control the variation of FF on short intervals. Differentiating FF and using 1+a​σj​cos⁡(ξj​x)≥1−a1+a\sigma_{j}\cos(\xi_{j}x)\geq 1-a, we find

|F′​(x)|≤a1−a​∑j=1Mξj.|F^{\prime}(x)|\leq\frac{a}{1-a}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\xi_{j}.

Since ξj≤Q−(M−j)​ξM\xi_{j}\leq Q^{-(M-j)}\xi_{M}, another geometric sum yields

Lip⁡(F)≤a1−a​∑j=1Mξj≤BQ,a​ξM.\operatorname{Lip}(F)\leq\frac{a}{1-a}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\xi_{j}\leq B_{Q,a}\xi_{M}. (2.4)

We now use these estimates to bound the entropy on a spatial grid. Let η=β−N\eta=\beta^{-N}, put K=⌊W/η⌋,Ck=[k​η,(k+1)​η),K=\lfloor W/\eta\rfloor,\ C_{k}=[k\eta,(k+1)\eta), and let UU be the union of the cells for which ℙ⁡(K=k)>0\mathbb{P}(K=k)>0. 0<ZU:=∫U𝒫⁡(x)​𝑑x≤∫−R−1R+1𝒫⁡(x)​𝑑x≤2​R+2+DQ,a.0<Z_{U}:=\int_{U}\mathcal{P}(x)\,dx\leq\int_{-R-1}^{R+1}\mathcal{P}(x)\,dx\leq 2R+2+D_{Q,a}.

For each occupied cell define qk=1ZU​∫Ck𝒫⁡(x)​𝑑x.q_{k}=\frac{1}{Z_{U}}\int_{C_{k}}\mathcal{P}(x)\,dx. These numbers are positive and sum to one.

Fix an occupied cell CkC_{k} and let y∈Cky\in C_{k}. For every x∈Ckx\in C_{k}, we have |x−y|≤η|x-y|\leq\eta. The Lipschitz estimate (2.4), together with η​ξM≤1\eta\xi_{M}\leq 1, therefore implies

F⁡(x)≥F⁡(y)−BQ,a​ξM​η≥F⁡(y)−BQ,a.F(x)\geq F(y)-B_{Q,a}\xi_{M}\eta\geq F(y)-B_{Q,a}.

Integrating over CkC_{k} gives

qk≥ηZU​exp⁡(F⁡(y)−BQ,a).q_{k}\geq\frac{\eta}{Z_{U}}\exp\!\bigl(F(y)-B_{Q,a}\bigr).

In particular, since W∈CKW\in C_{K} almost surely,

−log⁡qK≤N​log⁡β+log⁡ZU−F⁡(W)+BQ,a.-\log q_{K}\leq N\log\beta+\log Z_{U}-F(W)+B_{Q,a}.

The nonnegativity of relative entropy between the distribution of KK and the probability vector (qk)(q_{k}) gives H⁡(K)≤𝔼⁡[−log⁡qK]H(K)\leq\mathbb{E}[-\log q_{K}]. Taking expectations in the preceding inequality and using the bounds for 𝔼​F​(W)\mathbb{E}F(W) and ZUZ_{U}, we obtain

H⁡(K)\displaystyle H(K) ≤N​log⁡β−𝔼​F​(W)+log⁡ZU+BQ,a\displaystyle\leq N\log\beta-\mathbb{E}F(W)+\log Z_{U}+B_{Q,a}
≤N​log⁡β−M​Ψ​(a)+log⁡(2​R+2+DQ,a)+BQ,a.\displaystyle\leq N\log\beta-M\Psi(a)+\log(2R+2+D_{Q,a})+B_{Q,a}. (2.5)

It remains to pass from the grid entropy to HN=H⁡(XN)H_{N}=H(X_{N}). For this we use the separation of distinct atoms of XNX_{N}. Take two distinct values x,x′x,x^{\prime} of XNX_{N}. Their difference can be written as

x−x′=2​u,u=∑j=0N−1dj​β−j≠0,dj∈{−1,0,1}.x-x^{\prime}=2u,\qquad u=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}d_{j}\beta^{-j}\neq 0,\qquad d_{j}\in\{-1,0,1\}.

Since β\beta is an algebraic unit, β−1\beta^{-1} is an algebraic integer, and hence so is uu. At the other three embeddings, corresponding to β−1,ζ,ζ¯\beta^{-1},\zeta,\bar{\zeta}, we have

|∑j=0N−1dj​βj|<βNβ−1,|∑j=0N−1dj​ζ−j|≤N,|∑j=0N−1dj​ζ¯−j|≤N.\left|\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}d_{j}\beta^{j}\right|<\frac{\beta^{N}}{\beta-1},\qquad\left|\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}d_{j}\zeta^{-j}\right|\leq N,\qquad\left|\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}d_{j}\bar{\zeta}^{-j}\right|\leq N.

H⁡(XN∣K)≤log⁡(Csep​N2)=2​log⁡N+log⁡Csep.H(X_{N}\mid K)\leq\log(C_{\mathrm{sep}}N^{2})=2\log N+\log C_{\mathrm{sep}}.

By the chain rule,

HN=H⁡(XN)≤H⁡(XN,K)=H⁡(K)+H⁡(XN∣K).H_{N}=H(X_{N})\leq H(X_{N},K)=H(K)+H(X_{N}\mid K).

Combining this with (2.5) gives

HN≤N​log⁡β−M​Ψ​(a)+2​log⁡N+log⁡[(2​R+2+DQ,a)​Csep]+BQ,a,H_{N}\leq N\log\beta-M\Psi(a)+2\log N+\log\!\bigl[(2R+2+D_{Q,a})C_{\mathrm{sep}}\bigr]+B_{Q,a},

which is the first inequality in (2.1). The second follows from Ψ⁡(a)≥a2/2\Psi(a)\geq a^{2}/2.

3. Quartic Salem parameters and algebraic seeds

We use the reciprocal construction and controlled returns from [3, Sections 4–5]. The real embeddings give geometric tails, while the unit-circle pair contributes an oscillatory term. We first choose fixed power seeds and then use returns of the unit-circle conjugates to reduce the oscillatory term.

4. A reciprocal mirror and its action

For the remainder of the construction write d=|1−ζ2|d=|1-\zeta^{2}|. Subtracting a distant translate produces two copies of the old core, with a gap between them. A return of ζL\zeta^{L} towards one reduces the outgoing oscillation. We estimate the action in these three regions and in the two exterior tails. 6. Localized trajectories and the entropy deficit

We now restore the outgoing oscillation and apply the entropy estimate from Section 2. The argument uses the full localized action, a uniform bound for the real tail, and an expanding left coefficient bounded away from zero. These are also the quantities provided by the finite constructions in Appendix A.

For the centered trajectories constructed above, the required congruence already follows from (5.8). The following lemma gives an alternative criterion based on an integer recurrence and an exact left tail. It also applies to the Green-sequence construction in Appendix A.2.

Appendix C Exact arithmetic and reproduction

The companion archive contains the verification programs and three deterministic reports for the upper-bound certificates, algebraic seeds, and entropy bounds. The README.md file describes the contents of the archive and gives further instructions for running the programs. All finite checks can be reproduced by running the following command from the archive root:

python3 -S verification/verify_all.py

The program checks the archive manifest, recomputes the three mathematical reports, and compares them byte for byte with the supplied versions. It uses only Python’s standard library. All acceptance conditions are explicit and remain active under Python optimization, without relying on optional assert statements.

The numerical verification uses rational interval arithmetic with outward rounding. The fixed denominator is S=10200S=10^{200}, so every interval has endpoints in S−1​ℤS^{-1}\mathbb{Z}. Addition is exact on this grid. Multiplication and division use the extreme values at the interval endpoints, followed by outward integer rounding. Division is performed only when the denominator interval excludes zero, while square roots are enclosed using integer square roots of scaled endpoints. These operations ensure that the resulting intervals contain the exact values.

The algebraic roots are computed from the exact expressions

β=u+u2−42,r=u−u2−42,ζ=v+i​4−v22,\beta=\frac{u+\sqrt{u^{2}-4}}{2},\qquad r=\frac{u-\sqrt{u^{2}-4}}{2},\qquad\zeta=\frac{v+i\sqrt{4-v^{2}}}{2},

with (u,v)(u,v) given by (3.1). Complex numbers are enclosed by rectangular intervals, and large powers are computed by repeated squaring.

The transcendental functions are also enclosed by rational intervals. The bounds for π\pi follow from Machin’s identity

π=16​arctan⁡(1/5)−4​arctan⁡(1/239),\pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239),

using 160160 terms of each alternating series and bounding the remainder by the first omitted term. Sine and cosine are evaluated by 100100-term Taylor sums for arguments of modulus less than 22, with remainder bounds |x|201/201!|x|^{201}/201! and |x|200/200!|x|^{200}/200!, respectively. To evaluate the potential, let c=cos⁡(π​t)>0c=\cos(\pi t)>0 and z=(1−c)/(1+c)z=(1-c)/(1+c). Then

V⁡(t)=4​∑j=0159z2​j+12​j+1+R,0≤R≤4​z321321​(1−z2).V(t)=4\sum_{j=0}^{159}\frac{z^{2j+1}}{2j+1}+R,\qquad 0\leq R\leq\frac{4z^{321}}{321(1-z^{2})}.

This follows by expanding −2​log⁡c-2\log c and bounding the remaining positive terms by a geometric series. The program checks c>0c>0 and uses c≤1c\leq 1 when enclosing zz. Thus the transcendental estimates used in the verification have rigorous rational bounds.

The finite checks are carried out separately for the two polynomials. Canonical representatives are accepted only when both endpoints of their enclosing intervals determine the same centering integer and the centered interval lies strictly inside (−1/2,1/2)(-1/2,1/2). For P1P_{1}, the program evaluates the 2727 seed core potentials, verifies the finite forcing and the bounds needed for the exterior formulas, and applies (4.3) twice. For P2P_{2}, it evaluates the 28852885 seed core potentials, applies (A.5), and includes the stable tails through (A.10). The program also checks the left coefficients, return amplitudes, finite Fourier actions, and the inequalities in (B.3), (B.4), and (B.6).

Two further checks complete the verification. The algebraic-seed check establishes (A.2) and (A.8) using exact integer Laurent-polynomial arithmetic, including the index translations from the power seeds to the finite configurations. The entropy-bounds check takes the certified action, amplitude, and left-coefficient intervals as inputs, independently isolates the algebraic roots, and recomputes the rational entropy and dimension bounds. The upper-bound verification establishes the finite seed estimates and their propagation, while the entropy constant follows from the analytic proof of Corollary 2.2. The supplied reports are used only for comparison after the computations have been repeated.

The analytic estimates reduce the required computations to the finite seed evaluations, outward interval powers, and scalar inequalities. In particular, the verification does not require enumerating the large cores or the 2Ni2^{N_{i}} words at the entropy scales NiN_{i}.

Data and Code Availability

The certificate data and verification programs supporting the explicit Hausdorff-dimension bounds in Theorem 1.2 are openly available on Zenodo [2]. The archive contains the finite certificate inputs, verification code, recorded outputs, and instructions for reproducing all finite checks. The verification programs use exact rational interval arithmetic and the Python standard library, as described in Appendix C. The proof of Theorem 1.1 is independent of this archive.
